newsitem.title: UK: UK insurance tax hike seen less than expected.
newsitem.headline: UK insurance tax hike seen less than expected.

text.p: An increase in insurance premium tax (IPT) to four percent announced by UK chancellor Kenneth Clarke in his budget speech on Tuesday was less than the six percent expected by analysts and feared by the industry.
"It's an easy target, but four percent is not too stiff," said insurance analyst Tom Bennett at Paribas Capital Markets.
"It won't make any difference to insurers," he said.
Some of the heat came out of gains in insurance stocks after Clarke announced the increase, predicted as part of measures to finance a possible modest cut in income tax.
Commercial Union eased back to 673 pence, 19 up on the day, after earlier rising to a new year high of 696 during a flurry of activity in options.

IPT is levied on car and household insurance. It varies widely in other European countries, according to recent figures from industry association the Comite Europeen des Assurances (CEA), although in most it is higher than in the UK.

Car owners in most of the rest of Europe pay between seven and 18 percent on their motor premiums, although a few countries have no tax on motor insurance. Tax rates may also vary according to vehicle type.
Tax on household insurance ranges from zero in Sweden to 22 percent in Finland, with most European citizens paying between seven and 11 percent.
The Association of British Insurers (ABI) said it was "surprised, saddened and disappointed" at the increase in IPT from 2.5 percent to four percent.
"IPT is a regressive tax on the prudent," said the ABI's deputy general director Tony Baker. "Insurance is not a luxury and should not be taxed as such."
He said that the average UK household would now be paying one pound a week in insurance premium tax and a total of three pounds a week in government taxes and levies on insurance.
Baker added that Clarke was wrong to say non-life insurance was undertaxed. IPT is levied on car and household insurance.
